What is ByteQuay?

ByteQuay is a macOS desktop app for GitHub pull-request work and local coding agents. It brings repositories, reviews, tasks, and the context behind a change into one place.

What is its goal?

“Review is all you need” expresses the direction: spend more time understanding and deciding, with agents helping investigate, implement, and verify the work.

  • Keep work connected. Follow a change from an issue or goal through development, review, and delivery.
  • Make changes understandable. Read the code, checks, explanations, and discussion together.
  • Keep you in control. Choose what to run, accept, publish, and merge. Review automation choices before starting a task.
  • Keep the workspace close. App state and working copies live on your Mac. GitHub and model-provider requests still use external services.

Three useful concepts

  • A workspace is the home for one repository and its work.
  • A task is an agent conversation with its own working copy and execution history.
  • A goal describes what you want to achieve. Its work items track outcomes; a task is one attempt to produce an outcome.

ByteQuay is pre-1.0. These guides describe the current development version; installed releases may offer fewer controls. Start with one repository and one pull request.

Get started

  1. Install ByteQuay. Download the DMG from GitHub Releases, open it, and drag ByteQuay.app to Applications. Current builds require macOS 14+ and JDK 25; follow the instructions for your release.
  2. Connect GitHub. On the welcome screen, choose Use my GitHub CLI login. If needed, run gh auth login in Terminal and retry. Alternatively, enter a personal access token and choose Connect with token →. The app recommends a classic token with repo and read:user scopes.
  3. Watch a repository. From Home → Repos you watch → + Watch, search for a repository. Check the source branch, push destination, and PR destination, then choose Watch repository.
  4. Open a pull request. Open Pull requests, select Review or My work, and choose a PR. Read its checks and activity, then open WorkBench → Changes.
  5. Set up an agent when you need one. Install Codex or Claude CLI, then follow Agent tasks to sign in and select a model. GitHub connection and agent-provider sign-in are separate.

You can start by browsing and reviewing PRs without starting an agent task. Manage GitHub credentials later in Settings → Integrations → GitHub.

Code & Tests offers IDEA Light and Darcula themes with Atom One-style syntax colors, plus GitHub Dark with a dark canvas and GitHub-style syntax colors. License headers and imports fold on first open; expand them with the gutter arrows. Symbol search, callers, and usages remain available through the editor shortcuts and context menu. Press Shift twice or ⌘⇧F, or click Search, to open Search Everywhere. Exact class and file names rank first. Other results put normal classes before test classes, then fields and other symbols, files, and matching source lines. All combines a class and its matching source file into one result that opens the declaration. The popup shows up to 30 matches and skips content search when name matches fill it. Module names appear on the right; test-file rows are green. Filter with Classes, Files, Symbols, or Text. ⌘F opens the same popup for text in the current file, including unsaved edits. Use ↑/↓ and Enter to open a result, or Escape to close. Search respects project ignore and exclude settings; refine the query when results are limited. All favors names and source code; use Files for paths or Text to search other content, including fixtures and logs. Changing the query cancels the previous search; slow searches finish with the available results and a notice. ⌘-click a method to see its usages. A single usage opens directly; otherwise a popup lists filenames, line numbers, and source lines, with test-file results in green. Usages in the current file appear first while the rest of the project is searched. Usages inside library JARs and the JDK are not listed. Select a result to jump there, or press Escape to close the popup. If the language service is still preparing the project, the popup waits and runs the search automatically when it is ready. Java code is analyzed with the newest installed JDK, release 21 or later, so install the release your build plugins require. Working-copy reset and discard are in the … menu and require confirmation.

Use the play button beside a test in the editor to run or debug it. Run and Debug show their last selected or newly started tests with the output log. Each panel keeps its own history picker for earlier results. Debugging tests uses the supported test runner without a separate launch configuration.

Home and workspaces

Home shows your profile, contribution history, watched repositories, and recent activity. A repository workspace keeps its tasks, PRs, issues, commits, and memory together.

Workspace home always includes My PRs, with up to two of your open or draft pull requests. Unread updates appear first, followed by the most recently updated PRs. Opening a card keeps it in My PRs while the PR remains open. Use Snooze to hide it until the chosen time. These cards have no acknowledge action.

Updates to merged or closed PRs, including the merge or closure itself, appear in Needs attention until read or acknowledged.

  1. Choose Home → + Watch or Workspaces → New workspace, then select a repository.
  2. Choose Direct clone or Personal fork in the confirmation dialog. Private and internal repositories, and repositories you own, recommend direct clone. Public repositories owned by someone else recommend a personal fork.
  3. Direct clone follows the selected repository’s commits, issues and pull requests, and pushes work branches there. You need write permission to publish development changes; without it, you can still clone and follow the repository. Personal fork follows the upstream repository and publishes work branches to your own fork.
  4. Review Followed for updates, New branches start from, Work branches push to, and Pull requests open against, then choose Watch repository or Create fork and watch. Changing the workflow does not create a fork until you confirm.
  5. Open the workspace. Use its sidebar to switch between Tasks, Pull requests, Issues, Jira, Commits, and Memory. Commits becomes available after the repository has cloned.

Unwatch moves the workspace to Workspaces → Retired and retains local history. Use Watch again to resume following it. Delete… → Delete local data is a separate confirmed removal of local workspace data; it does not delete a GitHub repository.

Find and review pull requests

  1. Open Pull requests globally or within a workspace. Choose Review, Open, My work, Monitored, Reviewed, or Closed. Hidden tabs are available under More filters.
  2. Search by title, #number, or @author. Clear the search to return to the selected filter.
  3. Open a PR. PR contains its overview, checks, and activity. WorkBench → Changes contains changed files and commit selection.
  4. Select a diff line or range, write feedback, and choose Add to review. When ready, choose Submit review, inspect the pending comments, select Comment, Approve, or Request Changes where allowed, and submit.
  5. Use Monitor PR (the bell) to keep a PR in Monitored. Stop monitoring PR removes it from that list. Merged PRs cannot be monitored; monitoring stops automatically when ByteQuay detects a merge.

Post now publishes an individual comment immediately. Review submission and merge controls write to GitHub; inspect the outgoing content and selected action first. Your own PR cannot be self-approved.

On your own PR, Development task opens the linked conversation, including a completed task, or prepares one if none exists. Opening it does not start agent work. Review task opens the separate reviewer, including one started from the development task before publication, or starts a PR review if none exists.

Explore code locally

In a watched repository, open WorkBench → Code & Tests and choose Create worktree to explore. For an existing working copy, choose Start IDE if its code server is not running. Visiting the tab reuses a ready server; it does not start a new one without confirmation.

The IDE uses local memory and CPU, indexing takes time, and worktrees and index caches use disk space. Usage depends on the repository and languages. Opening the IDE does not start an AI agent or use model tokens.

Check failures and merging

Expand the failing-check group in PR, then choose Show log for a GitHub Actions job. Open in GitHub provides the complete log. Rerun failed tests appears when your permissions and the failed checks support it.

The header’s merge/check-status control shows the actions available for that PR, such as Ready for review, Rebase and merge, or Merge when ready. Monitoring with the bell does not enable automatic CI repair.

Ask for a private agent review

Use a private review to understand a change and investigate findings before deciding what to share. First watch the repository and configure a ready Review model in Settings → Agents → Models.

  1. Open a PR and select WorkBench → Summary → Start review.
  2. Read the change explanation and selected findings. Choose View in Changes to inspect the relevant code, or Ask reviewer to discuss a finding privately. Open Review details to inspect the recorded candidates, evidence, and coverage of behavior, interactions, and design. Progress checkpoints remain provisional until the review finishes; other recorded findings stay available in these details.
  3. Choose Add to my review to copy a finding into your editable pending review. Inspect it and use Submit review when you want to publish it.
  4. Use Update review after the PR changes. Later reviews refresh the findings and their supporting investigation. The saved change explanation stays attached to its original commits and reviewed head. Use the refresh icon beside Change intention to regenerate the intention and commit summaries from the latest committed version, independently of findings. The existing explanation stays visible until refresh succeeds. End review ends the reviewer task and releases its working copy; saved findings and discussions remain.

For development before a PR exists, open the task’s WorkBench → Summary → Review changes. This reviews committed changes, including unpushed commits; it excludes uncommitted edits.

Choose Request fix → Send to developer on a finding to ask its development agent to address it. The conversation shows a compact Fix the agent review card with the finding number and title. Click it to open the original finding, or expand its details to inspect the full instructions and review context.

The development agent can also read the saved findings itself, so you can ask in its task for several at once, such as “fix the open findings”. It reads the review of its own changes and the open reviews of its pull request; a later task on the same pull request reads them too. Its reply appears on the finding as Developer and stays private. It resolves a finding only after fixing it and replying; the card then says Resolved by Developer and you can Reopen it. A finding it rejects stays open with its reason, for you to decide. Update review still has the reviewer check the open findings.

Discuss without publishing

  • In a development task or review conversation, highlight text in a finished agent answer and choose Ask about this → Ask for a private side conversation. Reopen it from Discussions.
  • On someone else’s GitHub comment, Ask agent opens a private discussion beside the comment. Send your question to prepare the PR’s code context automatically; a full review is not required. Existing task or review context is reused. If setup is needed, use Watch repository or Model settings and return to your saved question. Starting a review later preserves the discussion.
  • Draft with agent fills an editable reply. It stays Draft · not posted until you choose Comment.
  • Resolve locally changes the private discussion or finding; it does not resolve a GitHub review thread.

Work with coding agents

Check account usage

Choose Usage at the bottom of the sidebar, then select an account. DeepSeek keys show the account’s available credit balance and warn when it is insufficient for API calls. Checks refresh while the panel is open and are cached for up to a minute. For other API-key providers, check the provider’s billing dashboard.

Connect a provider

You only need the provider you want to use: Codex, Claude, or a supported saved API key. A Claude account is not required for Codex or API-key tasks. New-task composers choose a ready provider when the configured default is unavailable; you can change that choice before sending. Drafting and Backport remain available while you set up a provider.

  1. Install the Codex or Claude CLI on your Mac, then open Settings → Agents → Models.
  2. Under Providers, choose Sign in if needed and complete sign-in. Choose Check and wait for Ready.
  3. Choose the Development model and a Review model, or Same as Development. Repository settings → Model overrides lets one repository use different choices.

Start a task

  1. Open a workspace’s Tasks → + New task.
  2. Describe the change in Let’s ship…. Include the outcome you want, relevant context, and how you will judge success. Select the provider and model.
  3. Open Automation and review the publication and CI choices described below. They lock after the task starts.
  4. Choose the upward Send arrow or press Enter. ByteQuay prepares a separate branch and working copy for the task. Shift+Enter adds a line; + attaches an image when the selected model supports it.

The initial branch name is provisional. Once the actual change is clear, the agent names it <username>/bytequay/<actual-change> before finishing its first development turn or pushing, for example chenjian2664/bytequay/convert-parquet-time-millis-to-micro. Renaming is available only during the first turn. If that turn ends without a concrete change, the initial name stays. Later turns always keep the branch name, even when it has not been pushed. Published branches and tasks imported from existing pull requests keep their names.

Guide the work

  • Steer sends information into the active turn when supported. Run next queues a later message; Resume queue continues a paused queue after you address its cause. Claude steering requires Claude Code 2.1.295 or newer. It delivers your update while the agent works; a command already running may finish before Claude acts on it.
  • On Approval needed, inspect the action and permissions, then choose Allow once, Allow for this task if offered, or Deny.
  • Use Stop this turn to interrupt the agent. Use Stop automation to stop delivery follow-up.
  • Inspect WorkBench → Changes and Summary before accepting the result. Code & Tests provides file browsing, an available targeted test runner, and a terminal; the built-in runner currently supports the Maven-wrapper profile. Gutter markers show added lines in green, updated lines in blue, and deletion points in red, compared with the base. They refresh after saving and hide while the editor differs from the saved file. Retained read-only files show the same markers.
  • When idle with its queue handled, choose Mark it complete (the checkmark) to finish the task. Archive moves it out of the active list; Delete separately removes its history and generated local work.

If sign-in expires, sign in again and refresh login status. Where offered, inspect Retry last message… before resending. A Delivery uncertain message needs inspection; it is not automatically resent.

App notices appear in the bottom-right corner when a task or review needs your attention or finishes a turn. While you’re viewing that task in the active ByteQuay window, its notices stay quiet, including while you scroll older messages or use its editor. They remain available in the Notices counter without popping up when you leave the task.

Reuse instructions

Open Settings → Agents → Skills → Add skill. Enter a name, choose Global, Development, or Review, write the instructions, and save. Changes apply from the next turn.

Deliver changes and repair CI

Before sending a new development task, open Automation. Finished development work is committed automatically. Publication depends on the choices you accept:

  • Auto draft PR pushes commits and creates or updates the task’s pull request. It is on by default.
  • Auto CI fix repairs supported failing checks, reruns CI, and can mark the draft ready when checks pass. It can write to GitHub and is on by default.
  • CI repair agent chooses the same agent as development or another supported agent.
  • Auto review summary adds a private note about new review comments. It does not post comments or fix code, and is off by default.
  • Keep commits local for this turn disables publication and CI follow-up for that submission.

Change defaults for new tasks in Settings → Agents → Workflow. A started task’s automation settings are read-only.

  1. Follow delivery and CI activity in the task header after development finishes.
  2. Type @ci followed by a text message to guide the running CI repair agent when its provider supports steering. When CI needs your input, the same action replies to the paused run and resumes it.
  3. Use Stop automation to stop the continuation. Review and merge the resulting PR yourself when it is ready.

Ordinary PR details do not have a general “Start CI Autofix” button. Reading logs or monitoring a PR does not authorize repairs.

Turn a goal into useful work

Goals help you clarify an objective, learn about a repository, and track whether the work actually achieved its intended result.

  1. Open a repository workspace and choose the floating Goal control, or press ⌥G.
  2. In Guide, answer What do you want to achieve? in your own words or use a suggested direction. Choose Send and answer the follow-up questions.
  3. Review the proposed objective, success definition, and constraints. Choose Accept goal, Adjust, or Skip.
  4. Review recommendations. Start opens the named lesson or starts the named investigation; development recommendations open a prepared composer for you to review and submit. Not now dismisses a recommendation.
  5. In Work, follow Next, Working, Blocked, and Done. Open an item to inspect its sources, attempts, and history.
  6. When the outcome is ready, enter the result, evidence, and scope covered, then choose Accept result. A finished task or closed ticket alone does not mark the work item done.

Learn and organize

For a proposed course, choose Accept course, open a lesson, read its explanation and exercise, and submit Your answer with Answer under Check. Ask questions beside the lesson and choose Mark lesson done when ready.

Work → New work item creates an outcome with a title, kind, and success condition. Add existing links issues, tickets, tasks, or PRs. Use Waits on to record a dependency. Pause guidance pauses suggestions; New goal in the GOAL menu starts another objective.

Keep related work together with Epics

An Epic connects a larger issue or ticket to the work needed to finish it. Its Work view shows progress, active attempts, and dependencies in one place.

  1. Open an Epic issue or Jira ticket and choose Work beside its source tab.
  2. When new source children are offered, inspect them and choose Sync to bring them into the Epic, or Not now to leave the suggestion for later.
  3. Add a work item by title, or choose Add existing to link an issue, ticket, pull request, or task. Review proposed work before choosing Accept.
  4. Open a work item to inspect its state and linked attempts. Choose Run on eligible work to start its development task at once and follow it in the task's conversation; the agent can read the Epic, its work list, and the item it is delivering. Dependencies explain what is waiting.
  5. Review completed outcomes. When the Epic is ready, choose Conclude Epic and record its outcome. Closing the source issue or ticket is a separate action.

Build repository memory

Memory stores sourced rules, useful commands, and specifications so agents can apply what has already been learned about a repository.

  1. Open the workspace’s Memory page and choose Learn from my PRs. You can also use Learn from this PR on a closed or merged PR.
  2. Inspect entries under Memories. Filter by Rules, Recipes, or Specs, then open an entry to read Applies to and Sources.
  3. Use Edit → Save, Delete, or Restore where available. Editing an entry makes it yours, so agents will not change it.
  4. Under Agents use memory in, select Reviews, Development tasks, or both. Inspect flagged entries under Needs you.

Check code against a specification

  1. Choose Memory → Check against spec, then select a module or enter a directory path.
  2. Select the linked pages to inspect, or use Add spec for an additional specification URL.
  3. Choose Reproduce up to and start Check against spec with a ready agent provider.
  4. Open the report under Spec checks and inspect each Failing test and Issue draft.
  5. Choose Open issue to open a prefilled GitHub issue form. Inspect and submit it there yourself, or use Copy body or Dismiss.

Only reproduced findings are shown as confirmed gaps. Unreproduced candidates and already-reported issues remain separate. Stop check stops a running investigation.

Work items: local, GitHub, and Jira

Use existing issue or ticket context as the starting point for development, so the task stays connected to the requested change.

Local work

Open Work items → Local, add the context and acceptance criteria, then choose Start development. The workspace's configured Development agent starts and its task opens directly, without an extra Send step. The agent reads the saved work-item context and, when present, its parent Epic's link, description, and related work. Missing or stale parent context is identified in that read.

GitHub issues

Open a workspace’s Issues, find the issue, and choose its Start development action when available. Review the prepared task composer and submit it. View task returns to linked work; New issue begins a new issue.

Jira

  1. Open Settings → Integrations → Jira → Add account. Enter the Jira site, Atlassian account email, and API token, then choose Connect account. Follow Required token permissions for the required scopes.
  2. Open Jira and use Site, board and sprint to choose a board and sprint or Backlog.
  3. Browse Current sprint or Completed. Use Assigned to me, Status, Search tickets, and List or Board to find the work.
  4. Open an eligible unfinished leaf ticket and choose Start development. Select and Assign workspace if prompted, then review and submit the task composer.
  5. Use View task to return to development. Ticket field edits, comments, and status transitions are separate user actions.

Open in Jira handles fields and operations the app does not support. Browser sign-in is shown only when configured. Replace an expired token in settings.

Move changes between branches

Cherry-pick commits

  1. Open Commits → History. Check the first repository/branch control: it is the destination. Select the source with the second control.
  2. Choose commits or use Select range, select the endpoints, then choose Cherry-pick.
  3. Review the route, commit order, and conflict resolver. Remove unwanted commits, then choose Start cherry-pick (N).
  4. If it pauses, use Send note or Cancel execution. Find existing executions in Commits → Cherry pick.
  5. After completion, use Deliver this generated branch → Push branch, then Create pull request, with the displayed confirmations. PR creation also authorizes the disclosed CI monitor.

The initial cherry-pick runs locally. Dry run shows the execution plan; it does not run another Git simulation.

Backport through related workspaces

  1. Watch the involved repositories. In each destination’s repository settings, open Related workspaces → + Add related workspace.
  2. Select the source workspace, choose Fork, and enable Use as default backport source to include this destination when no targets are named. Choose Add. Each destination can have one default source. A Dependency permits investigation but not backporting.
  3. On Workspace Home or Tasks, click Backport beside the repo icon, or type @backp and select the @backport suggestion with Enter, Tab or a click. Add owner/repo #1234 and send it. Start backport conversation on the Backport chains tab also fills the composer. Use @backport #1234 when the source is unambiguous. Name destinations to override the default route. You can also describe a fix and request backports before its PR exists.
  4. Follow Tasks → Backport chains or the conversation’s chain card. Inspect linked PRs and use Stop, Resume, or Select commits when offered.

Each step waits for its source PR to merge and uses its landed changes. Forks sharing a source can run in parallel; nested forks wait for their parent. If “then” conflicts with the saved route, the agent asks which source and order you intend. ByteQuay never merges these PRs automatically.

Follow people with Circles

Circles are personal collections of people whose work you want to follow. Creating one does not invite or notify anyone.

  1. Open Circles → Create a circle, or New circle from its menu.
  2. Enter a name, optionally add a description, choose People, and optionally scope it to Repositories. Select Create circle.
  3. Use Needs you, Activity, Members, and Insights to follow the collected work. Shortcuts ⌘1–⌘4 switch views.
  4. Open relevant work, acknowledge it, or Snooze it. Choose a time range and inspect the activity behind insight counts.
  5. Use Refresh activity for another collection pass and inspect Updated or Partial for coverage.

The people picker searches contributors cached from watched repositories. Circles do not grant repository access. Their insights reflect collected activity, not a complete measure of someone’s work.

When something needs attention

  • GitHub will not connect: retry the GitHub CLI login or update the token in Settings → Integrations → GitHub. Check repository access when using a fine-grained token.
  • An agent is unavailable: open Settings → Agents → Models, sign in, choose Check, and wait for Ready. Check the workspace’s model override too.
  • Commits or files are unavailable: wait for repository preparation. Code & Tests needs an existing task or review working copy.
  • A queue is paused: address the displayed cause, then Resume queue. Inspect uncertain delivery before sending the same message again.
  • A feature differs from this guide: check your release version and its release notes. Some controls depend on repository permissions, provider capabilities, or the state of the selected work.

For architecture and product boundaries, read the high-level design. For building from source, use the repository’s CONTRIBUTING guide.
